experiment.plan: Arm the collectors and run for five 300 s collection cycles, then finalize. Fleet held at 20,250 devices, the first rung the 400-thread knee search failed: the queue stands at 4,400 to 6,900 thirty minutes after the search's window, pool 400/400, Core CPU 96-99%, achieved rate about 67/s against 67.5 required. The search climbed from 17,250 in steps of 500 (all pass to 19,750 at CPU 94.5%) on a Core restarted at 10:12Z for the aligned-schedule test at 19,250, which passed. Core: procfs 5 s and sysstat only, GC log via jcmd VM.log (running since the 10:12Z restart), one jcmd Thread.print by hand mid-window; no JFR and no jcmd snapshots because both collapsed this Core at 17,250 (pm-snmp-agent-latency-32g-live results-attempt1 and results-attempt2). Minion: JFR profile, jcmd snapshots 60 s, perf 99 Hz, procfs, sysstat, pcap ring on every interface. Collectd threads=400 (was 300 for the earlier searches), G1, 20 GiB heap, max-repetitions 5, netem delay 75ms 25ms on netsim enp6s19.
experiment.question: What are Core and the Minion doing over five collection cycles at 20,250 devices, the first rung the 400-thread search fails on the 32 GiB Core, and what relates the thread count, the eight vCPU and the heap to that knee?

figures.title: Collections completed per second against the rate the fleet requires
figures.note: Achieved sits 1.2% under required for the whole window: the collector is at capacity and the shortfall is what the queue accumulates.

figures.title: Collectd pending queue, rolling one-minute peak and floor
figures.note: The floor never touches zero and both lines climb about one task a second: a slow runaway, the difference between demand and capacity.

figures.title: Collectd thread pool occupancy against its 400-thread ceiling
figures.note: 400 of 400 in every sample. With the processor at 96% the pool is full because collections take longer, not because 400 is too few.

figures.title: CPU busy: Core, Minion and database
figures.note: The Minion carries its own capture in this window; unobserved it reads about 53%. The database serves 10,800 transactions a second at 53%.

figures.title: Core JVM heap against its 20 GiB ceiling, old-generation collections and young-collection time
figures.unit: GiB, per minute, and s per minute
figures.note: Five old-generation collections in the window, the spikes on the per-minute line, each a full stop of up to 6.4 s; none at any rung to 19,750. Young collections cost 3.5 s of pause per minute, 5.8% of wall, up from 4.1% at 17,250: the allocation rate follows the collection rate and the live set follows the fleet and the pool.

figures.title: Context switches per second: Core, Minion and database
figures.note: The Core's 47,000 a second are mostly the 400 collection threads waking from database round trips; the database's 50,000 are the other end of the same transactions.

figures.title: One-minute load per vCPU, every collection VM
figures.note: The Core's run queue holds about 54 runnable threads for 8 cores. Everything else is under 1.2 per vCPU.

figures.title: The 400-thread search, 17,250 to 20,250: Core CPU and pool occupancy
figures.note: Each plateau is one rung's 15-minute window; the dips are the grow-and-scan phases between rungs and the 09:45 to 11:05 gap is the restart test at 19,250. CPU climbs 2.5 to 4 points per 500 devices while the pool mean climbs from 321 to 400.

figures.title: The 400-thread search: pending queue, five-minute peak and floor
figures.note: The floor stays at zero on every rung to 19,750 and lifts off at 20,250. The spikes between rungs are the imports of 500 nodes.

figures.title: The 400-thread search: Core load and context switches
figures.note: Context switches stay near 47,000 a second on every rung: they scale with the collection rate, which barely moves. Load doubles from 30 to 56 as the run queue fills: that is the processor saturating, not the threads waiting.

figures.title: Database connection pool on the Core during collection
figures.note: 162 transactions per collection: the node lookup per resource in the Kafka producer, plus the collection's own. The pool of 250 peaks at 121 active.

figures.title: Kafka segment: Minion RPC responses and Core producer
figures.note: 429 Mbit/s on the broker: SNMP results as formatted XML from the Minion, the same bytes into the Core, and the Core's protobuf metrics out.

answers.question: Where is the knee with 400 threads, and what binds there?
How do the thread count, the eight vCPU and the heap relate to each other and to the knee?
What do load, context switches on wait, agent latency and PDUs per collection say about where the time goes?
What does the failing rung look like over five cycles?
Is anything else in the lab near a limit?
What moves the knee from here?

gaps.question: Is the knee a hard failure or a soft one?
gaps.why: The pass rule requires the queue to touch zero inside the window. At 20,250 it never does, but the collector still completes 98.8% of the required rate; the queue grows about one task a second and the effective interval, once the queue saturates, is about 304 s against 300. The rule detects the capacity crossing; the consequence at this rung is a 1.2% stretch, not a collapse.

gaps.question: Was the Core in the same state on every rung?
gaps.why: OpenNMS was restarted at 10:12 for the aligned-schedule test at 19,250, between the 19,250 and 19,750 rungs. Rungs from 19,750 up ran with the schedule aligned in one wave per cycle; rungs to 19,250 ran on a Core restarted at 06:51 whose wave had spread. The aligned schedule holds the pool full for a third of each cycle and the per-rung CPU figures above 19,250 carry that.

gaps.question: Does the Minion's own capture change what the Minion figures say?
gaps.why: The Minion carried JFR, jcmd snapshots, perf and three pcap rings during the window. It reads 64% of four vCPU with them and about 53% without, from the search's per-rung averages. Nothing ran on the Core JVM.

gaps.question: Are the per-thread context switch figures representative?
gaps.why: They come from one 60 s sample of /proc/<pid>/task/*/status taken by hand at 13:06, inside the window. The system-wide rate from node_exporter agrees within 25% (47,000 against 60,600 inside the JVM for that minute), and the per-rung averages show the rate is flat across the search, so the split by thread group is taken as typical.

gaps.question: Does a uniform 50 to 100 ms per response stand for a real fleet?
gaps.why: netem delays every SNMP response by a uniform 50 to 100 ms. The thread arithmetic in this report uses the measured 4.74 s per collection on the wire; a fleet with a different latency shape needs its own number in the same formula.

gaps.question: Is the CPU cost per collection a constant?
gaps.why: It is read as CPU busy times cores divided by the achieved rate on seven rungs and lands between 0.110 and 0.116 core-seconds every time. That is one fleet, one data collection package with 144 interfaces per device and one RPC encoding; a different package changes the number, not the arithmetic.
